title: The Big Bang to a Living Planet

cards.h: Everything you know started as a tiny, hot dot
cards.b:
Imagine every star, every river and every chai cup you have ever had. All of it was once squeezed into something smaller than an atom. That is where our story starts.

We will cover 13.8 billion years in a few minutes. Do not worry about memorising dates. Just enjoy how strange it all is.

About 13.8 billion years ago, space itself began to expand from an extremely hot, dense state. We call this the Big Bang. For the first few hundred thousand years, the universe was a glowing fog.

Then it cooled. Hydrogen and helium gathered into clouds. Gravity pulled the clouds together until they ignited. The first stars were born.

cards.h: You are made of dead stars
cards.b:
The Big Bang made mostly hydrogen and helium. Heavier things, like the iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones, were cooked inside stars. When big stars exploded, they scattered those atoms across space.

Our Sun and its planets formed from such a cloud about 4.6 billion years ago. Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.

Early Earth was a ball of fire and rock. Most scientists think a Mars-sized body, often called Theia, smashed into it. The debris became our Moon. This is the giant-impact idea, and it is the best-supported explanation we have.

The Moon steadies Earth's tilt. That helps keep our climate calm enough for life.

The first living things were tiny single cells. Evidence for life goes back at least 3.5 billion years. Some of these microbes, cyanobacteria, learned to make food from sunlight and gave off oxygen.

Oxygen was poison for most life then. Around 2.4 billion years ago it built up in the air in the Great Oxidation Event. It changed the planet for ever.

The Cambrian explosion, about 540 million years ago, filled the seas with complex animals. An asteroid struck near today's Mexico 66 million years ago and wiped out the non-bird dinosaurs. Mammals got their chance. In cosmic terms, humans arrived just now.

cards.h: Was the Big Bang an explosion in space?
cards.b: Myth: a bomb went off in an empty room.Fact: there was no room. Space itself expanded everywhere at once. There is no centre you can point to. Another common mix-up: the Big Bang does not explain why it happened. Science can describe what happened very soon after, but the very first moment remains an open question.

Five things to remember

  1. The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago; Earth about 4.5 billion.
  2. Heavy elements were made inside stars, so we are made of star material.
  3. Our Moon most likely came from a giant collision.
  4. Oxygen from cyanobacteria changed the air about 2.4 billion years ago.
  5. Humans appeared only about 300,000 years ago.

Think about it

  • If the whole history were one year, humans arrive on the last evening. What does that do to how you see history?
  • Why might the Moon matter for life?

quiz.q: How old is the universe, roughly?
quiz.w: Current measurements give about 13.8 billion years.

quiz.q: The Big Bang was best described as...
quiz.w: Space itself expanded; there was no outside to explode into.

quiz.q: Where were iron and calcium mostly made?
quiz.w: Stars forged heavy elements; supernovae spread them.
Earth formed around 4.5 billion years ago.

quiz.q: What is the leading explanation for the Moon's origin?
o: A giant impact with a Mars-sized body
Earth spun it off like a drop
quiz.w: The giant-impact idea is best supported.

quiz.q: Which microbes pumped oxygen into the air?
quiz.w: They did photosynthesis and gave off oxygen.

quiz.q: What ended the non-bird dinosaurs 66 million years ago?
o: An ice age caused by humans
quiz.w: The Chicxulub impact near today's Mexico.
The collision began about 50 million years ago.

quiz.q: Which Rigveda hymn wonders who truly knows how creation began?
